hero.headline: Fort Pierce woman accused of stealing $60,000 from bingo hall where she worked
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce woman has been arrested after authorities say she stole approximately $60,000 from the bingo hall where she worked, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

The theft occurred over a six-month period, the sheriff's office reported. Management at the bingo hall discovered financial irregularities in the facility's records, which prompted an investigation into the missing funds.

The woman was taken into custody Friday on grand theft charges. Specifically, she faces charges of grand theft over $20,000, a felony offense in Florida. Investigators determined that the suspect had systematically taken money from the business during her employment at the facility.

The sheriff's office conducted a thorough investigation that eventually led to the woman's arrest. She was booked into custody and is currently being held pending court proceedings on the theft charges.

The bingo hall where the theft occurred has not been publicly identified by authorities. The investigation remains ongoing with the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

As of the latest reports, authorities have not disclosed whether additional charges may be filed against the suspect or if other individuals may be involved in the theft scheme. The case is still under review as prosecutors prepare for court proceedings.

This arrest adds to recent criminal activity reported in the Fort Pierce and St. Lucie County area. The case highlights concerns about internal financial controls at businesses that handle large amounts of cash, particularly entertainment venues like bingo halls.

Bingo halls typically handle substantial daily cash transactions from players, making them vulnerable to employee theft if proper accounting procedures and oversight are not in place. The discovery of this alleged theft suggests that management implemented financial monitoring systems that eventually caught the discrepancies.

The suspect's arrest marks the conclusion of the sheriff's office investigation into the missing funds. She will appear in court to face the grand theft charges. Depending on the outcome of her case, she could face significant prison time if convicted, as grand theft over $20,000 is treated as a serious felony offense under Florida law.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has not released the suspect's name or additional details about her employment history at the facility. Her arraignment and future court dates will determine the next steps in the legal process.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce pastor arrested after police find children starving in filthy home

Authorities documented the conditions inside the home as part of their investigation. The evidence gathered pointed to patterns of neglect and abuse affecting multiple children under the pastor's supervision and care.

Police intervened after receiving information concerning the welfare and living conditions of the children in the household. Upon arrival, officers found conditions that prompted immediate action to ensure the safety of the minors present.

The children have been removed from the home and placed in protective care. All minors who were residing at the residence at the time of the discovery have been relocated away from the environment where they were allegedly neglected.

The pastor now faces criminal charges related to child abuse and neglect. The specific charges reflect the severity of the conditions police documented during their investigation.

Investigators are working to determine how long the conditions persisted before authorities were alerted to the situation. The timeline of events and the full scope of alleged mistreatment remain under active investigation as police gather additional evidence and conduct interviews.

The case highlights the responsibilities of foster parents and those in positions of trust within religious communities. The arrest has drawn attention to child welfare oversight in the area and the mechanisms through which concerned individuals can report suspected abuse.

Fort Pierce police have urged anyone with additional information about the case to come forward. Authorities continue to piece together details about what occurred inside the home and any factors that may have contributed to the neglect of the children.

The investigation is ongoing as police work to ensure all aspects of the case are thoroughly documented. Prosecutors will review the evidence gathered by law enforcement to determine the appropriate legal proceedings moving forward.

This case serves as a reminder of the importance of child protection services and the vigilance required to identify and intervene in situations involving vulnerable minors. The children involved are now receiving care and support as they recover from their experience.

cards.headline: Jupiter Island erosion threatens to split island at Peck Lake
cards.teaser: Jupiter Island's shoreline has eroded so severely that the ocean could break through at Peck Lake, according to a 2025 state environmental report. A town official says the response amounts to reapplying a Band-Aid.
cards.body:
The 2025 Florida Department of Environmental Protection report found Jupiter Island's 11.5-mile shoreline has eroded so severely the ocean could break through at Peck Lake. A Jupiter Island official says the town is reapplying a Band-Aid to address the erosion crisis.

The erosion poses an existential threat to the barrier island. If the ocean breaks through at Peck Lake, it would physically split Jupiter Island into separate sections and fundamentally alter the island's geography.

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection documented the critical erosion conditions along the entire 11.5-mile shoreline. Jupiter Island officials are working to respond to the threat, though the town official's Band-Aid comment suggests current measures may not be adequate to prevent a breakthrough.

cards.headline: Governor DeSantis Property Tax Plan Could Cut School Funding by $1 Billion in South Florida
cards.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has proposed a property tax amendment that would significantly alter Florida's tax structure, with analysis indicating South Florida schools could lose approximately $1 billion in funding if voters approve the measure.

The proposal, often referred to as "Save Our Homes," would expand property tax breaks for homeowners with primary residences while potentially shifting the tax burden to owners of second homes and commercial properties. The initiative aims to address affordability concerns for Florida residents dealing with rising property values and increasing insurance costs.

Education officials across South Florida have expressed serious concerns about the plan's impact on school districts. The region's school systems in Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties rely heavily on property tax revenue to fund daily operations, pay teachers, and support educational programs. Any substantial reduction in this revenue stream could force difficult decisions about resource allocation and services.

According to available analysis, the tax changes would disproportionately affect South Florida's school districts, which collectively serve hundreds of thousands of students. School administrators have begun examining various budget scenarios to prepare for potential revenue losses if voters approve the constitutional amendment in the upcoming election.

The DeSantis administration has framed the property tax relief as an essential response to affordability pressures facing homeowners. Supporters argue the measure would help residents manage their property tax obligations during a time of significant economic strain in the state's housing market.

The proposal requires approval through a constitutional amendment, meaning it must be submitted to Florida voters for final decision. This requirement has allowed time for affected parties, including school districts and education advocates, to conduct detailed analyses of the potential fiscal consequences.

School leaders and education advocates continue to assess the full scope of how the tax changes would affect classroom resources, teacher recruitment and retention, and overall district operations. The $1 billion figure represents a substantial portion of South Florida school funding and would require significant adjustments to education budgets across the region.

The debate over the property tax amendment reflects a broader tension in Florida between providing tax relief to homeowners and maintaining adequate funding for essential services like public education. As voters prepare to weigh in on the proposal, education officials remain focused on documenting and communicating the potential impact on students and schools.

The constitutional amendment process ensures the issue will receive public attention and debate before any changes take effect, allowing stakeholders throughout South Florida to participate in the decision-making process about the state's tax policy and education funding priorities.

cards.body:

The seasonal ban protects local waterways during Florida's rainy summer months, when excess nutrients can runoff into rivers, lagoons and coastal waters. This helps prevent algae blooms and water quality degradation. Residents and landscaping companies must comply with the prohibition or risk fines. The ban lifts October 1, allowing fertilizer use to resume for fall and winter.

hero.headline: Governor DeSantis Property Tax Plan Could Cut School Funding by $1 Billion in South Florida
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis has proposed a property tax amendment that would significantly alter Florida's tax structure, with analysis indicating South Florida schools could lose approximately $1 billion in funding if voters approve the measure.

The proposal, often referred to as "Save Our Homes," would expand property tax breaks for homeowners with primary residences while potentially shifting the tax burden to owners of second homes and commercial properties. The initiative aims to address affordability concerns for Florida residents dealing with rising property values and increasing insurance costs.

Education officials across South Florida have expressed serious concerns about the plan's impact on school districts. The region's school systems in Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties rely heavily on property tax revenue to fund daily operations, pay teachers, and support educational programs. Any substantial reduction in this revenue stream could force difficult decisions about resource allocation and services.

According to available analysis, the tax changes would disproportionately affect South Florida's school districts, which collectively serve hundreds of thousands of students. School administrators have begun examining various budget scenarios to prepare for potential revenue losses if voters approve the constitutional amendment in the upcoming election.

The DeSantis administration has framed the property tax relief as an essential response to affordability pressures facing homeowners. Supporters argue the measure would help residents manage their property tax obligations during a time of significant economic strain in the state's housing market.

The proposal requires approval through a constitutional amendment, meaning it must be submitted to Florida voters for final decision. This requirement has allowed time for affected parties, including school districts and education advocates, to conduct detailed analyses of the potential fiscal consequences.

School leaders and education advocates continue to assess the full scope of how the tax changes would affect classroom resources, teacher recruitment and retention, and overall district operations. The $1 billion figure represents a substantial portion of South Florida school funding and would require significant adjustments to education budgets across the region.

The debate over the property tax amendment reflects a broader tension in Florida between providing tax relief to homeowners and maintaining adequate funding for essential services like public education. As voters prepare to weigh in on the proposal, education officials remain focused on documenting and communicating the potential impact on students and schools.

The constitutional amendment process ensures the issue will receive public attention and debate before any changes take effect, allowing stakeholders throughout South Florida to participate in the decision-making process about the state's tax policy and education funding priorities.

hero.headline: Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties implement summer fertilizer ban through September
hero.teaser: A ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen for lawns and landscaping took effect June 1 across Martin, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.
hero.body:
Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties have enacted a ban on fertilizers containing phosphorus or nitrogen from June 1 through September 30. The restriction applies to both residential homeowners and commercial landscaping operations throughout all three Treasure Coast counties.

The seasonal ban targets the summer months when heavy rainfall increases the risk of nutrient-rich runoff flowing into local waterways. These excess nutrients can trigger algae blooms that damage the environment and public health.

Jordan Skaggs, an environmental resources specialist with St. Lucie County, explained the reasoning behind the restriction. "It can shade out beneficial plants to fish and wildlife," Skaggs said. "At certain densities, harmful algae blooms can release toxins that can affect human health, wildlife health and overall ecosystem health."

The ban specifically protects sensitive waterways including the Indian River lagoon and St. Lucie River. During the rainy season, nutrient runoff from lawns and landscaping can wash into these ecosystems, accelerating algae growth and degrading water quality.

Residents and landscaping companies cannot apply nitrogen or phosphorus fertilizers to any lawns or landscaping during the four-month period. This applies regardless of whether the fertilizer is being used for residential gardens, commercial properties, or any other landscaping purpose.

Despite the restriction, property owners still have options for maintaining healthy landscapes during the summer months. Grantly Ricketts, director of the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences St. Lucie County Extension, recommends composting as an effective alternative.

"It can be like a small trash can," Ricketts said. "That is the easiest and most practical way or means to add nutrients to your landscape."

Composting allows homeowners to create their own nutrient-rich soil amendment using kitchen scraps and yard waste. This approach maintains landscape health without introducing synthetic fertilizers into the environment. The composting method provides a sustainable solution for gardeners and landscapers who need to nourish their plants during the summer ban period.

The three-county restriction reflects growing efforts to protect Florida's waterways from nutrient pollution. By limiting fertilizer applications during the season when rainfall and stormwater runoff are heaviest, the counties aim to reduce algae blooms and preserve aquatic ecosystems.

Residents who need to maintain their landscaping during the ban should consult local extension services for approved methods and timing recommendations. The temporary restriction runs through September 30, when the rainy season typically begins to decrease.

The venue serves as both an active business and a tribute to the region's citrus farming tradition, integrating the area's agricultural history into its daily operations.

cards.headline: Sebastian River High School Football Game Against Legacy Scheduled
cards.teaser: Sebastian River High School faces Legacy in football on October 9.
cards.body:
Sebastian River High School has a football game scheduled against Legacy on October 9. The matchup is part of the Sebastian River football schedule for the upcoming season.

Sebastian River High School serves students in Sebastian and surrounding areas of Indian River County, where the school's football program competes against regional teams.
